published.title: Smart Home Automation for Beginners: Your First 5 Routines
published.excerpt: New to smart home automation? Start with these five practical routines - morning lighting, away mode, appliance scheduling, wind-down and security check-ins - using gear that suits Australian homes.
published.content:
The best way to start smart home automation is with a handful of simple routines rather than dozens of gadgets. A morning lighting scene, an away mode, scheduled appliances, an evening wind-down, and a security check-in cover most beginner needs and teach you how triggers, conditions and actions actually work together. ## Why Start With Routines, Not Gadgets It's tempting to buy every smart device at once, but automation only feels useful once devices talk to each other on a schedule or trigger. A single smart bulb that you still turn on manually every night isn't really "smart" yet - it's just a bulb you paid more for. Routines are what turn individual devices into a system. Starting with five core routines also keeps the learning curve manageable. You'll get comfortable with one app or hub, understand how triggers and conditions work, and build confidence before layering in more complex automations like [Zigbee mesh networks that reach the garage or granny flat](https://nxtsmarthome.com.au/setup-guides/zigbee-mesh-garage-granny-flat-double-brick-home). ## What You Need Before You Automate Anything ### Choosing a Hub or Controller Most beginner routines can run through a manufacturer's app alone, but you'll hit limits quickly once you mix brands. A dedicated hub or controller lets devices from different ecosystems - lighting, plugs, sensors and cameras - work together in one routine instead of three separate apps. The Nabu Casa Home Assistant Green Plug-and-Play Hub is worth considering if you want a single system that can eventually manage lighting, climate, plugs and sensors together, without being locked into one brand's app. It runs Home Assistant OS out of the box, which is genuinely beginner-friendly to set up, though it does involve more initial configuration than a single-brand app if you're used to something like a basic plug app. For a household planning to expand automation over time, that flexibility tends to pay off. ::product:nabu-casa-home-assistant-green-plug-and-play-hub:: ### Wi-Fi, Zigbee and Matter, Briefly Devices connect in different ways: Wi-Fi devices talk directly to your router, Zigbee devices form their own low-power mesh network via a hub, and Matter is a newer standard designed to let devices work across ecosystems more easily. You don't need to master the technical detail to get started, but knowing which protocol a device uses helps you understand why some things need a bridge or hub and others don't. If devices ever start dropping off your network, [troubleshooting Wi-Fi dropouts](https://nxtsmarthome.com.au/setup-guides/fix-smart-home-wifi-dropouts) is a good next stop. ## Routine 1: Good Morning Lighting A morning routine that gradually brings lights up to a comfortable level (rather than snapping on at full brightness) is one of the most satisfying first automations. It's also a good entry point because lighting is usually the easiest device category to automate reliably. If you're using Philips Hue bulbs, the Philips Hue Bridge (V2) is essentially required to unlock full routine features and scheduling in the Hue app, plus it enables Matter integration if you want to bring Hue lighting into a broader ecosystem later. Without the bridge, some Hue bulbs can still work over Bluetooth in a limited way, but you lose the scheduling depth and reliability that make morning routines worthwhile. The trade-off is one more piece of hardware plumbed into your router, but for most households it's a one-off setup step. ::product:philips-hue-bridge-v2:: A simple version of this routine: lights at 20% brightness five minutes before your alarm, rising to 80% over the next ten minutes on weekdays only. Skip weekends unless you want an argument with your household. ## Routine 2: Leaving Home / Away Mode Away mode is usually triggered by your phone leaving a geofenced area, or manually via a single tap or voice command. A good beginner away routine might turn off non-essential plugs, switch lights to an away-simulation pattern, and arm your indoor camera. For the camera element, the Ring Indoor Cam (2nd Gen) is a compact option worth considering for renters or apartments where a hardwired outdoor camera isn't practical or permitted under a strata scheme. It includes a manual privacy shutter, which is a genuinely useful feature for an indoor camera - you can physically block the lens when you're home and don't want it recording, rather than relying solely on app settings. It's an indoor-only camera, so it won't cover outdoor security needs on its own. ::product:ring-indoor-cam-2nd-gen:: Before fitting any camera, check your strata by-laws or rental agreement if it faces communal areas or a neighbour's property - this is a common point of dispute in apartment buildings and isn't something a manufacturer's app can resolve for you. ## Routine 3: Appliance Scheduling With a Smart Plug Smart plugs are one of the cheapest ways into automation because they don't require any fixed wiring - just plug them into an existing 240V outlet and pair them with an app. The SwitchBot Smart Plug Mini AU is a straightforward option that works over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi within the SwitchBot ecosystem, suiting things like scheduling a fan, lamp or space heater on a timer. ::product:switchbot-smart-plug-mini-au:: The main trade-off with a standalone smart plug is that it's easiest to automate on its own schedule; cross-device routines (like "turn off the heater when everyone leaves") generally work better once the plug is connected through a hub alongside your other devices. If you're also interested in tracking appliance energy use against solar export or time-of-use tariffs, it's worth reading how to [build a Home Assistant energy dashboard](https://nxtsmarthome.com.au/setup-guides/home-assistant-energy-dashboard-solar-export-time-of-use-tariffs) once you're past the beginner stage. Never use a smart plug to control anything beyond its rated load, and don't attempt to modify or hardwire a plug yourself - any fixed wiring work should go to a licensed electrician, and it's worth understanding [what smart home electrical work you can legally do yourself in Australia](https://nxtsmarthome.com.au/setup-guides/smart-home-electrical-work-australia-legal) before you start. ## Routine 4: Evening Wind-Down A wind-down routine dims lights, lowers any smart blinds, and can nudge your climate control toward a night-time setting, all triggered by a set time or a voice command like "goodnight." This is where a hub becomes genuinely useful, because you're coordinating lighting and climate together rather than one device type in isolation. If your reverse-cycle split system already has app or voice control fitted, this is a natural point to loop it into the same evening routine - see [setting up voice and app control for a reverse-cycle split system](https://nxtsmarthome.com.au/setup-guides/reverse-cycle-split-system-voice-app-control-without-replacing) for the setup process without replacing the unit. ## Routine 5: Security Check-In When You're Not Home This routine is less about constant monitoring and more about a quick, on-demand check - a single tap in your app that shows you the live camera feed and confirms lights and plugs are in the state you expect. It's a good complement to Routine 2, giving you a manual fallback rather than relying purely on automated triggers. ## Renters and Strata Considerations Most of the devices covered here - smart plugs, plug-in cameras, bulbs that fit standard fittings - don't require any fixed wiring, which makes them a reasonable starting point for renters. Strata buildings may still have rules about cameras facing shared areas, external fittings, or Wi-Fi extenders in common corridors, so it's worth checking your by-laws before installing anything visible from outside your unit. When in doubt, favour indoor, plug-in, battery, or app-removable devices over anything fixed to walls or ceilings. ## Common Beginner Mistakes A few habits derail most first-time automation setups: naming every device "Plug 1," "Plug 2" and forgetting which is which within a week; building overly complex routines before mastering simple ones; and skipping firmware updates, which can cause devices to behave unpredictably. Start with the five routines above, get each one reliable, and only then start layering conditions like sunset time or occupancy sensors on top.

faq.question: Do I need a hub to start automating my home?
faq.answer: Not strictly - many smart plugs, bulbs and cameras work fine through their own app for basic schedules. A hub becomes useful once you want devices from different brands to trigger each other, such as a camera detecting motion and turning on a light. Beginners can start app-only and add a hub later.

faq.question: What's the difference between Zigbee, Wi-Fi and Matter devices?
faq.answer: Wi-Fi devices connect directly to your router, Zigbee devices form a separate low-power mesh that usually needs a hub or bridge, and Matter is a newer standard designed to let devices from different brands work together more easily. You don't need to choose one exclusively - many households end up with a mix.

faq.question: Can renters set up smart home routines without breaching a lease?
faq.answer: Generally, plug-in and battery-powered devices that don't involve fixed wiring or permanent fittings are lower-risk for renters, but tenancy agreements and strata by-laws vary. It's worth checking your specific lease terms and, for anything involving cameras or shared areas, confirming with your landlord or body corporate first.

faq.question: Why does my smart light or plug keep disconnecting from Wi-Fi?
faq.answer: Common causes include router placement, network congestion, or too many devices on an older Wi-Fi band. If this becomes a recurring issue, a dedicated troubleshooting guide on fixing devices that keep dropping off Wi-Fi can help narrow down the cause before you start replacing hardware.

faq.question: Is it safe to leave smart plugs running appliances while I'm away?
faq.answer: Smart plugs are designed for standard household loads within their rated limits, but they're not a substitute for basic appliance safety - don't use them with heaters or appliances not designed for unattended use, and always follow the manufacturer's guidance. If you're unsure about a specific appliance, a licensed electrician can advise.

faq.question: What should my very first automation be if I only set up one?
faq.answer: A morning or evening lighting routine is usually the easiest starting point because lighting is simple to automate reliably and the payoff is immediately noticeable. It also teaches you the basic trigger-condition-action structure that every other routine on this list builds on.
